## Simple explanation

Version control keeps a history of project changes so a team can see what
changed, compare versions, and safely collaborate.

## Technical explanation

Distributed version control systems such as Git store snapshots and metadata
in a repository. Branches allow independent work; commits record changes; and
merges integrate histories. Version control tracks text and other files, but
large model artifacts and datasets often need specialized storage or registry
systems.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Reproducible AI work depends on more than model code. Versioning code,
configuration, data references, and evaluation procedures helps explain how
results were produced and supports rollback when a change degrades behavior.

## How it works

Developers edit files, review diffs, stage relevant changes, and create commits.
Branches isolate work until it is reviewed and merged. Tags or release
references can mark source states associated with deployed models or
experiments.

## Practical example

When changing a feature pipeline, create a branch, commit the transformation
and its tests, and record the dataset and model versions used in evaluation.
This makes it possible to compare the new pipeline with the previous one.

## Common misconceptions

- A Git commit does not automatically version data stored outside the
  repository.
- A commit alone does not ensure a run is reproducible; dependencies,
  configuration, randomness, and data must also be tracked.
